title: monotonic stacks and monotonic queues
concepts: A monotonic stack keeps candidate values or indices in nondecreasing or nonincreasing order by removing candidates made permanently irrelevant by a new element.
The stack's invariant and the strictness of its comparison determine how equal values are handled; duplicates can change the answer if the inequality is chosen incorrectly.
For next-greater or next-smaller questions, scanning direction and whether unresolved indices remain on the stack define which future or previous candidate is found.
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so a nested while-loop can still produce linear total work through aggregate analysis.
A monotonic deque tracks candidate indices for a moving range, evicting expired indices from the front and dominated candidates from the back.
Sliding-window extrema use a deque whose values remain monotonic and whose indices preserve expiration order; storing indices handles duplicate values and window boundaries.
Histogram area and subarray-minimum counting use nearest smaller boundaries, with tie-breaking rules needed to assign equal-valued ranges exactly once.
The structures are useful when a query asks for a nearest extremal candidate or a sliding-window extremum; they do not replace a general-purpose stack, queue, heap, or range-query structure.
